children: Protocol-driven emergency systems can help hospitals reduce critical delays in heart attacks, strokes and major trauma through faster triage, diagnostics and coordinated specialist response

On World Patient Safety Day, the focus on safer, timely and coordinated healthcare is especially relevant in the emergency medicine department, where every second & every minute can matter. In emergencies such as heart attacks, strokes and major trauma, treatment delays can have significant consequences. As hospitals strengthen emergency-care systems, protocol-driven pathways are increasingly being used to help teams identify high-risk patients quickly, prioritise investigations and activate the appropriate specialists without unnecessary delays.

Unlike routine medical care, emergency medicine often requires decisions to be made within minutes, sometimes before a complete diagnosis is available. A patient arriving with chest pain, sudden weakness or injuries after an accident may require assessment, imaging, laboratory investigations and specialist intervention almost simultaneously.

For hospitals, this is creating greater emphasis on structured triage, rapid diagnostics, pre-hospital coordination and multidisciplinary emergency response. Dr. Sujay Patil, HOD & Emergency Medicine Specialist at Apollo Hospitals, Pune, said, “Protocol-driven emergency care helps clinicians rapidly identify life-threatening conditions, prioritise the most time-sensitive investigations and involve the appropriate specialist teams early. In conditions such as stroke, cardiac emergencies and major trauma, this structured approach can reduce avoidable delays between a patient’s arrival, diagnosis and definitive treatment in Golden-Hour.”

The importance of such systems is particularly evident in stroke care. Establishing when the patient was last known to be well or normal, conducting an early neurological assessment and obtaining brain imaging can help clinicians determine the appropriate treatment pathway because TIME IS BRAIN and every minute 2 million neurons-brain cells die.

In acute cardiac emergencies, rapid ECG assessment can help identify patients who may require urgent coronary intervention. For major trauma, structured assessment allows emergency teams to simultaneously evaluate airway, breathing, circulation and potentially life-threatening bleeding-hemorrhage control.

Protocol-driven emergency medicine does not mean every patient receives identical treatment. Instead, it establishes predefined pathways for different clinical emergencies while allowing doctors to adapt treatment according to the patient's condition.

The approach can also extend beyond the emergency department. Pre-Hospital Care being’s through Hospital On Wheels means Ambulance. Ambulance teams can begin assessment and stabilization before hospital arrival and at patient doorstep and communicate critical information to the receiving Emergency Department Command Centre through 1066 SMART Ambulance.

Advance communication can allow emergency departments to prepare imaging, blood products, operating theatres, Cathlab or specialist teams before the patient arrives. For hospitals, this can shift emergency care from a largely reactive model towards a coordinated system in which multiple teams are activated around the same clinical objective.

As emergency departments become more protocol-driven, hospitals could increasingly track where time is being lost. Metrics such as arrival-to-ECG time, door-to-imaging time, specialist response time and time to definitive treatment can help identify operational bottlenecks. Digital triage, electronic alerts and integrated hospital information systems (EMR – HIS) could also support faster communication between emergency physicians and specialist departments.

However, technology alone cannot solve emergency-care delays. Hospitals still require trained emergency personnel 24x7 , appropriate diagnostic infrastructure, critical-care capacity and specialists who can respond around the clock. Building these systems can require greater investment in Emergency Medicine Physicians, nurses, ambulances, paramedic’s, diagnostic facilities, trauma infrastructure and critical-care resources.

The potential economic implications extend beyond the emergency department, as delayed treatment for heart attacks, strokes, serious trauma & other emergencies can result in longer hospital stays, rehabilitation requirements, disability and productivity losses including patient deaths. This means that improving emergency response is not simply about reducing the time a patient spends waiting. It is also about reducing delays at each stage of the clinical care pathway.

As Pune's healthcare infrastructure continues to expand, Emergency Medicine Department is increasingly becoming a coordinated system rather than a single department. For patients with a heart attack, stroke or major trauma, the focus is on recognizing the emergency early, activating the appropriate pathway and moving from assessment to definitive care as efficiently as possible.
Guest Author Critical Care & Emergency Medicine Specialist, Apollo Hospitals Pune.
